title: Statistics and Distributions
scope: Summarize data, measure spread, and reason from samples without hiding important variation.
beginnerEntry: You understand events, probability, and ordered numeric observations.

objectives: Compute and interpret center and spread.
Connect statistics to data preparation and model evaluation.

steps.prompt: Compare datasets [5,5,5,5,5] and [1,3,5,7,9]. They share a mean. What crucial information does the mean hide?
Why might median be safer than mean for incomes, and what does spread add to a claim about a typical value?
Predict how adding one value of 100 changes the mean, median, range, and overall shape of [1,2,3,4,5].
A distribution records how values occur. Center summarizes location; variance or standard deviation summarizes spread; samples estimate a larger population with uncertainty.

Five friends report commute times [20, 25, 25, 30, 90]. Compute mean and median, decide which honestly describes a typical commute, and explain what the 90 is doing to the average. Find one average quoted around you this week and ask what it hides.
A product page shows 4.2 stars. Behind it, one product has mostly 4s and 5s; another has half 5s and half 1s. Same average, opposite stories. The distribution, not the summary, is the truth.
A model is trained on data collected only from weekday daytime users. What can it honestly claim about weekend night users, and why does no amount of data volume fix a biased sample?

Sensor readings cluster near 50 with a few spikes at 500. Predict how the spikes distort the mean, which summary a monitoring dashboard should show, and what a model trained on raw values might wrongly learn.

Data preparation is applied statistics: distributions reveal outliers and skew before training, feature scaling uses mean and standard deviation, and evaluation compares distributions of errors, never a single flattering number.

Summarize [2,3,3,4,8] with mean, median, and range, describe its shape in words, and name one sampling risk if these were training rows. Notice the limitation: statistics describes data that already exists, but prediction needs to know how one quantity responds when another moves. That is the derivative.

measurement.prePrompt: Describe how you would summarize a list of measurements and what might be lost in one average.
measurement.postPrompt: Compare two datasets with the same mean but different spread, choose useful summaries, identify an outlier, and explain a sample-to-population risk.
successCriteria: Connects summary choices to a data or model decision.

misconceptions: A large sample is automatically representative.
reasoning.tutorGuidance: Have the learner compare raw values or a simple number line before calculating. Ask what each summary preserves, what it hides, and how collection choices could bias the sample.
